output.title: Focus blocks start with one recurring workflow
output.body:
Before you protect a focus block, decide what is actually breaking it.

For a small business owner, the useful question is not whether AI sounds smart. It is whether one recurring task keeps interrupting the day: repeated customer questions, invoice data entry, or lead follow-up. If the work changes every time, it is probably not the first thing to automate. If it shows up in the same shape again and again, that is a workflow worth looking at.

A simple check is enough: does the task follow a pattern, repeat weekly, and have a clear input and output? That is the threshold. It does not tell you to automate; it tells you whether the task deserves a closer look before you spend your focus block trying to “create” time out of thin air. Owners usually do enough spreadsheet heroics already.

That is the bounded decision Bareni starts with: identify one recurring workflow, then decide whether it should stay manual, be shared with a hire, or be scoped for automation. The normal sequence is to identify the workflow honestly, say whether AI fits, and then define a pilot scope if it does. Those timings are intended scopes, not guarantees.

The next practical step is simple: name the one task, note how often it interrupts your week, and check whether it repeats in a pattern before you protect the block.
